preamble: Vocalization of the velar stop [k] to the labio-velar glide [w]. The clearest case is Klingenheben's law in Hausa, under which syllable-final velars became [w] (*ɓáknáa > ɓáunáa 'buffalo'), while the same consonant stays [k] where it is an onset (plural ɓákàanée). In Australia, word-initial *k became w before *u in Nhanda (wuna < *kuna 'excrement') and in the Atampaya dialect of Uradhi (wumpu < *kumpu 'urine').

examples.note: Klingenheben's law (velar rule): a syllable-final velar becomes w; it stays k in the plural ɓákàanée, where it is an onset.
The intermediate *jǐw-náa was reinterpreted with long uu; unsuffixed jìkíi 'body' keeps the k.
Initial *k became w before *u; before other vowels it is usually lost (ami < *kami, ari < *kari).
The Angkamuthi dialect has umpu, with the stop lost.

sources: Newman, P. (2004). Klingenheben's Law in Hausa. Rüdiger Köppe. https://lccn.loc.gov/2005390185
